title: How can two fractions look different but be equal?
objective: Explain equivalent fractions by partitioning the same whole into more equal parts without changing the shaded amount.
successEvidence: The learner identifies and explains a new equivalent-fraction pair using equal-sized wholes and matching shaded area.

steps.title: Fractions need equal parts
steps.body: A fraction describes equal parts of one whole. If the pieces are different sizes, counting them cannot tell us a fraction of the whole.

steps.title: Shade one of two equal parts
steps.body: Split one bar into two equal parts and shade one. The shaded amount is one half.

model.label: The whole and shaded amount stay fixed

steps.title: Cut every half into two equal pieces
steps.body: The same bar now has four equal parts. The shaded half contains two of those fourths. No shaded area was added or removed.

steps.title: Different counts, same amount
steps.body: One half and two fourths use different-sized parts, but they cover the same length of an equal whole. That makes them equivalent fractions.

steps.title: Each old part was split into the same number of pieces
steps.body: To change thirds into sixths, split every third into two. The number of shaded pieces and the total number of pieces both double, so the amount stays equal.

steps.title: Repartition the same whole; preserve the amount
steps.body: Equivalent fractions can name the same amount with different equal-sized parts. Check them with equal wholes and matching shaded area.

model.label: Same whole + same shaded area = equivalent

checks.prompt: Which must be true before the pieces can represent a fraction?
checks.successMessage: Ready. Fraction parts must be equal parts of the same whole.
checks.explanationPrompt: Explain why unequal pieces cannot be counted as equal fractional parts.

choices.text: The pieces are equal in size
Every piece has a different colour
choices.feedback: Colour can help us see pieces, but it does not define a fraction.
choices.misconception: Uses appearance instead of equal partitioning

choices.text: There are more than two pieces
choices.feedback: A whole may be split into two equal parts. The important condition is equal size.

checks.successMessage: Yes. Splitting every fourth into two makes eight equal parts, with six shaded: 3/4 = 6/8.
checks.explanationPrompt: Explain what happened to both the numerator and denominator.

choices.feedback: The denominator changed but the numerator did not, so the shaded amount became smaller.
Adding one to both numbers does not preserve the same shaded proportion.
choices.misconception: Adds the same number instead of scaling both numbers

checks.successMessage: Correct. Every third was split into two, so 2/3 = 4/6.
checks.explanationPrompt: Justify the match using the same whole and shaded area.

choices.feedback: That keeps two shaded pieces while making each piece smaller, so it is only one third.
Those fractions do not cover the same proportion of an equal whole.
choices.misconception: Chooses nearby numbers without preserving proportion

checks.prompt: Tomorrow: which fraction is equivalent to 3/5?
checks.successMessage: Correct. Splitting every fifth into two gives 6/10 without changing the amount.
checks.explanationPrompt: Describe how each fifth was repartitioned.

choices.feedback: The parts became smaller but the shaded count did not change, so the amount was halved.
Adding one to both numbers does not preserve the same fraction.
choices.misconception: Adds the same number instead of scaling
